Pitched
picht
v. (past of pitch)
Past tense of pitch, Middle English picchen, to thrust in, to fix, to set firmly. Webster 1828: to throw or thrust; to fix; to set in array; to fix a tent or temporary habitation. In the Authorized Version the word belongs almost entirely to tents — and therefore to the whole doctrine of dwelling, from Abram’s canvas to the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched.

Biblical Definition

Pitched is a tent word, and in Scripture tents are never merely shelter; they are a confession about where a man belongs. Abram and Lot part, and the narrator marks the difference in one clause: Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:12). Nobody pitches a tent by accident. The direction of the door is the direction of the heart, and Lot’s door faced the city he would eventually have to be dragged out of. Jacob, returning, pitched his tent before the city of Shechem (Genesis 33:18). Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp (Exodus 33:7) — a pitching that was itself a judgment, putting the meeting place outside a people who had just made a calf. Then Hebrews takes the humble verb and gives it to God: Christ is a minister of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man (Hebrews 8:2). Every tent Israel ever staked was a copy. The original was pitched by God, and John says the Word did the same thing in flesh when He dwelt — tabernacled — among us.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PITCH as a verb: to throw or thrust; to fix or plant; to set in order or array; and specifically, to fix or set a tent, to encamp. PITCHED is its past tense and participle: fixed, planted, set in array, encamped.

expand to see more

PITCH, v.t. — To throw or thrust; to fix or plant; to set, as a tent or temporary habitation; to set in array; to regulate or set, as a tune. PITCHED, pp. — Set; planted; fixed; encamped; set in order.

Webster’s first sense is force and his second is permanence, and the Authorized Version needs both. A tent is pitched by driving something into the ground. The paradox of the patriarchs is that the most portable dwelling in the ancient world is fixed by an act of hammering — which is exactly the life of faith Hebrews 11 describes: staked down hard, and still not home.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 8:2 — "A minister of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man."

Genesis 13:12 — "Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom."

Exodus 33:7 — "And Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp, and called it the Tabernacle of the congregation. And it came to pass, that every one which sought the LORD went out unto the tabernacle of the congregation, which was without the camp."

Genesis 33:18 — "And Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Padanaram; and pitched his tent before the city."

Modern Corruption

Pitched is corrupted when the patriarchal tent is romanticized into a picture of spiritual freedom from commitment, and when Hebrews 8:2 — the tabernacle which the Lord pitched, and not man — is read as a metaphor rather than as the argument for the obsolescence of the whole earthly sanctuary system.

expand to see more

There is a familiar devotional use of the patriarchs’ tents that turns them into a warrant for rootlessness — travel light, hold nothing, keep your options open. Scripture’s point is nearly the opposite. Abraham was not uncommitted; he was committed to a city he could not yet see, and the tent was the cost of that commitment, not its reward. Hebrews 11 says plainly that he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God. The tent testifies to a settled hope, not a loose grip. Lot proves the point negatively: he is the one who kept his options open, pitched toward Sodom, and ended up with neither the tent nor the city.

The heavier misreading falls on Hebrews 8:2. When the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man is taken as poetic language for God’s nearness, the letter’s central argument is lost. The writer is making a structural claim: the earthly sanctuary was a copy and shadow, and the arrival of the real one renders the copy finished. That is why he can say the first covenant is decaying and ready to vanish away. Any theology that keeps a standing earthly priesthood, a repeated propitiatory sacrifice, or a mediating altar has not reckoned with the verb. The Lord pitched the true tabernacle. Man’s pitching is over.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Three Hebrew verbs and one Greek verb stand behind pitched. The Hebrew divides between stretching a tent out, dwelling in one, and encamping with a company — and the Greek word for the tabernacle God pitched is the ordinary word for driving a stake.

expand to see more

Hebrew nātāh (H5186) — to stretch out, to extend, to spread a tent (Exodus 33:7, Moses pitched it without the camp).

Hebrew āhal (H167) — to pitch a tent, to move a tent, to dwell in tents (Genesis 13:12, Lot pitched his tent toward Sodom).

Hebrew chānāh (H2583) — to encamp, to pitch camp as a company (Genesis 33:18, Jacob before Shechem).

Greek pēgnumi (G4078) — to fix, to fasten, to pitch (Hebrews 8:2, the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched).

Usage

"Pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:12) — the direction of the door is the direction of the heart."

"Moses pitched the tabernacle outside the camp (Exodus 33:7); the location of the meeting place was itself a verdict on the camp."

"The true tabernacle is the one which the Lord pitched, and not man (Hebrews 8:2) — every stake Israel drove was a copy of it."
